Targeted prints of matching rows, in the style of SAS PROC PRINT with WHERE

Source: R/proc_print.R
proc_print.Rd

Counts the rows that match each of a set of named conditions, and prints the matching rows to the console. It is the checking step a programmer runs after a build: write the build, cross-tab, spot a discrepancy, print the rows that look wrong. One call takes several conditions, as several SAS PROC PRINT; WHERE steps would.

Usage

proc_print(data, where, var = NULL, max_rows = 25L, console = TRUE)

Arguments

data

A data frame.

where

A list of conditions, each condition ~ "Label" with a single non-empty quoted label, or one such formula. Labels must be unique.

var

Character or NULL. Columns to print for the matching rows, SAS VAR. NULL prints every column.

max_rows

A single positive whole number. At most this many matching rows are printed per condition; the count is always the full count.

console

A single TRUE or FALSE. FALSE writes nothing, neither rows nor the warnings a condition raises, and only returns the counts.

Value

A data frame with one row per condition and the columns label, n (rows matching) and n_missing (rows for which the condition was NA). Both counts are integer. The matching rows are written to stderr() as a side effect and are not part of the result.

Details

Matching rows go to the console, and only counts reach a report. A targeted print shows patient rows, and a rendered report gets shared. So the rows are written to stderr(), which knitr and Quarto do not capture: an interactive session shows them, and a render leaves them out of the HTML whatever the chunk's message or warning options say. What the function returns, and what a report prints, is one count per condition. This is where it differs from SAS, whose PROC PRINT output is the listing.

Each condition is written condition ~ "Label", the shape of a bd job's EXCLUDE rules, and is evaluated with the columns of data in scope, then the formula's environment. A condition that evaluates to NA for a row does not match it; those rows are counted in n_missing, so a check that cannot be decided for some patients says so instead of reading as clean. A condition that fails is an error naming its label. The error does not repeat R's own message, which can quote a data value. Warnings and messages raised while a condition is evaluated (a date parser listing the value it could not read, say) go to stderr() with the rows, for the same reason.

See also

proc_freq, followup_check

Examples

dta <- generate_survival_data(n = 200, seed = 42)

# proc print; where age > 80; var age dead;
proc_print(dta,
  where = list(age > 80 ~ "Older than 80",
               dead == 1 & iv_dead < 1 ~ "Death in the first year"),
  var = c("age", "dead", "iv_dead"))
#>                     label n n_missing
#> 1           Older than 80 1         0
#> 2 Death in the first year 5         0
